decisions.decision: The deliverable is a single native SwiftUI iOS app with a real backend — no portfolio/multi-app interpretation.
decisions.rationale: Prompt uses singular 'app' throughout with no quantity language.
rejected_alternatives: Building multiple small concept apps to hedge risk
constraints: Later phases must not split scope into multiple unrelated apps

decisions.decision: Todo lists, habit trackers, journaling apps, and AI-wrapper apps are banned as the core offering, including disguised reskins of them.
decisions.rationale: Explicitly forbidden in the prompt; reskins would violate the spirit even if not the letter.
rejected_alternatives: Allowing a reskinned habit tracker with social features bolted on
constraints: A candidate concept must be checked against this list before being accepted

decisions.decision: Production-readiness is defined by checkable behaviors, not aesthetics: real empty/loading/error states verified under airplane mode and on a fresh zero-state account, session persistence across force-quit, and no UI claiming Saved/Synced/Sent without real backend acknowledgment.
decisions.rationale: Prevents 'production-shaped' from being quietly redefined down to 'compiles and has a login screen'; matches this factory's recorded history of placeholder/blank-screen failures.
rejected_alternatives: Treating production-readiness as a subjective/aesthetic judgment call
constraints: Every stateful screen must expose all four states before any later phase can claim it done

decisions.decision: The backend requirement must be provably load-bearing: the core value must fail or degrade for a solo user on one device with no second account/device involved.
decisions.rationale: Prevents a bolted-on Firebase/API call from satisfying 'genuinely requires a backend' while the real experience is single-player.
rejected_alternatives: Accepting any app with a network call as satisfying the backend requirement
constraints: Verification must include a live two-account/two-device test, not just an API existing

decisions.decision: The care-and-handoff relay concept for parents/guardians is carried forward as the working concept, provisionally, not as an immutable lock — it proceeds subject to a rollback gate if it fails the two-device/backend-load-bearing test or the safety constraints below.
decisions.rationale: Resolves the round-1 phase-boundary disagreement: Codex wanted to commit now, Claude wanted concept-commitment treated as a distinct later step; both agreed a provisional-but-testable commitment satisfies both concerns.
rejected_alternatives: Treating the concept as fully and finally locked in this phase with no further challenge
Deferring all concept discussion to a separate phase with no candidate carried forward
constraints: Any later phase must be able to reject or revise this concept if it fails the load-bearing backend test or safety constraints
Rollback must be explicit and documented if the concept is abandoned

decisions.decision: Matching is restricted to a pre-established trust graph (existing contacts, or verified members of a school/daycare pod a parent explicitly joins) — never open proximity-matching with unknown strangers.
decisions.rationale: Removes the core safety liability of algorithmically pairing a child handoff with an unvetted stranger, while preserving every backend-necessity argument (live availability, real-time acceptance, capacity/routing logic).
rejected_alternatives: Open proximity-based matching with nearby unknown users
Leaving matching scope unspecified and deciding it ad hoc during build
constraints: Data model and matching logic must enforce trust-graph/pod membership as a hard filter, not a ranking signal

decisions.decision: No UI element may imply identity verification, background-check completion, or safety vetting that the app does not actually perform; self-reported or peer-vouched trust must be labeled plainly as such.
decisions.rationale: Prevents a decorative 'Verified' badge or trust score from being mistaken for real vetting in a context (child handoff) where that mistake is dangerous, not just misleading.
rejected_alternatives: Using unqualified 'Verified Guardian' badges based only on self-reported profile fields
constraints: Design review and copy review must check every trust-related UI element against this rule before it ships

decisions.decision: Proof that a real backend endpoint is deployed and reachable from the iOS client is required as the first deliverable of the next (architecture/build) phase, before any concept-specific schema or screens are trusted as real.
decisions.rationale: Both participants agreed 'genuinely requires a backend' is meaningless if reachability is never actually confirmed in this build environment; discovering this at final verification would be too late.
rejected_alternatives: Assuming backend reachability and confirming it only at final verification
constraints: No feature-specific screen work should be considered validated until this reachability proof exists

decisions.decision: Naming and pitch framing must lead with the trust-graph/pod mechanic, not generic 'matching' language.
decisions.rationale: Leading with 'matching' makes the pitch sound like derivative 'Uber for childcare,' which is both less clever and more alarming than the actual trust-graph-constrained mechanic.
rejected_alternatives: Pitching the app primarily around real-time matching/availability without foregrounding the pod/trust-graph structure
constraints: Onboarding copy, app name, and marketing-style pitch language must foreground pod/trust-graph membership as the distinctive mechanic

decisions.decision: The concept is framed as a micro-supply network for immediate care continuity among people who already know each other, not a marketplace, matching app, or social-discovery product.
decisions.rationale: Keeps later phases from drifting toward marketplace/feed/discovery patterns that don't fit the trust-graph constraint from prompt_contract.
rejected_alternatives: Framing as a childcare marketplace or matching service
constraints: Naming, copy, and IA in later phases must reflect trust-transfer/coordination, not marketplace or social discovery

decisions.decision: The first build supports exactly one pod type: school pickup. Daycare and activity pod types are excluded from v1.
decisions.rationale: Each additional pod type multiplies onboarding/verification surface (different join stories per context) before the core relay loop is even proven once; narrowing maximizes the chance of a fully-working, well-tested first version.
rejected_alternatives: Supporting school, daycare, and activity pods in parallel from v1
constraints: Data model's pod entity should not be built polymorphic for multiple pod types until school-pickup is proven
Later phases may propose additional pod types only as an explicit v2+ extension

decisions.decision: No GPS/live location tracking or ETA-aware map features in v1.
decisions.rationale: Location features add real complexity (background location, permission UX, denied/restricted error states) and risk causing the app to be perceived as a worse Life360, for a decision pod members can make themselves in seconds.
rejected_alternatives: Including 'ETA-aware' matching or live location pins as a v1 differentiator
constraints: No location permission request in v1
Any future location feature must be proposed explicitly as v2+, not folded in silently

decisions.decision: No child PII (names, photos, face data) is stored or displayed in v1; requests reference the child generically.
decisions.rationale: Sidesteps a compliance/sensitivity problem nobody asked the team to solve, and isn't needed to route or complete a relay request.
rejected_alternatives: Storing child name/photo to personalize the request card
constraints: Data model and API contract in the next phase must not include child name/photo fields as required data

decisions.decision: The accept flow's race condition (multiple pod members accepting near-simultaneously) is a named first-build acceptance criterion: server-side first-accept-wins via a real conditional/compare-and-swap update, with the losing acceptor receiving an explicit 'already claimed' state and sub-30-second propagation to both devices in the happy path.
decisions.rationale: This is the concrete, testable mechanism that differentiates the app from a group chat; without a real server-arbitrated lock, the app's core value proposition silently fails under normal multi-person usage.
rejected_alternatives: Treating race-condition handling as an implementation detail left to the architecture/build phase without an explicit requirement or test case
constraints: A named test case must exist and be run: two authenticated devices racing an accept on the same request must resolve to exactly one winner and one clean rejection
This must appear in the API contract and be verified before the corresponding screens are considered done

decisions.decision: The audit/evidence log entry and the shareable 'relay receipt' are the same underlying data object, presented as two views: an internal audit record (requester, accepter, timestamps, consent) and a derived, privacy-filtered shareable summary card with no child name or address.
decisions.rationale: Avoids building two separate features for what is functionally one data object; delivers both the safety/audit requirement from prompt_contract and the viral/growth mechanic from a single data model decision.
rejected_alternatives: Building the audit log and the shareable receipt as two independent features/data objects
constraints: Data model in the next phase must define one artifact with a privacy-filtered projection for sharing, not two parallel entities

decisions.decision: Pod joining uses an invite-link or admin/pod-issued join code, with a real 'not in a pod yet' empty state and a clear CTA to join or start a pod — not a workflow that dead-ends for users without pre-existing pod membership.
decisions.rationale: Keeps the pod-gated design narrow and safe while avoiding an onboarding trap where a first-time user with no pod can do nothing at all.
rejected_alternatives: Requiring pre-existing pod membership with no in-app path to join or create one
constraints: Onboarding funnel in later phases must include a working join/create-pod path reachable from a zero-state account

decisions.decision: Cold-start/network-density viability will not be proven within this build cycle; instead, the mitigation is minimizing marginal join friction (one link, one tap, Sign in with Apple) and requiring a second real seeded pod-member account as a first-class part of this app's own verification protocol.
decisions.rationale: There is no way to seed a realistic 15-20 family classroom pod in a prototype build; the honest response is to optimize what's actually controllable (join friction) and to ensure verification actually exercises multi-user behavior rather than assuming it works.
rejected_alternatives: Treating cold-start as solved because a two-account demo passes
Ignoring cold-start risk entirely as out of scope for this phase
constraints: Verification/build phases must include a second real seeded account in the same pod as a required test step, not an afterthought

decisions.decision: This is a single-app build with no portfolio split — exactly one selected app, pulse-relay.
decisions.rationale: The original prompt uses 'app' singular with no quantity language, consistent with DEC-prompt_contract-001; the relay concept's mechanic (one trust graph, one request feed, one accept/conflict-resolution flow, one shared audit/receipt object) is not decomposable into independent sibling apps without breaking the core value proposition.
rejected_alternatives: Splitting into sibling apps by role (e.g. separate requester app and helper app)
A companion pod-admin app alongside the core app
Multiple concept apps hedging risk (group-chat clone, caregiver marketplace, emergency-alert app)
constraints: No later phase may introduce a portfolio_json manifest or sibling child projects for this build
All feature work stays within one Xcode project

decisions.decision: The selected app is named/framed as: slug pulse-relay, category real-time trust-graph coordination/social-utility, promise centered on fast pod-wide pickup coverage with exactly one confirmed acceptor, target user a parent/guardian in a specific school-pickup pod facing a same-day pickup conflict, build=true.
decisions.rationale: Both participants independently converged on this same framing; it matches the naming guidance from prompt_contract (lead with trust-graph/pod mechanic, not generic 'matching') and the locked scope from product_research (school-pickup-only, one pod type).
rejected_alternatives: Framing the category as marketplace or matching service
Framing the category as generic messaging/coordination without the trust-graph distinction
constraints: Naming, onboarding copy, and pitch framing in later phases must stay consistent with this framing

decisions.decision: If build time is constrained, cuts must come from secondary screens (pod management, profile/settings) before ever reducing the correctness or responsiveness of the two locked core funnels (post relay request; accept/conflict-resolve/complete).
decisions.rationale: The core loop's trustworthiness is the entire value proposition — a parent who receives a wrong or ambiguous 'who's got my kid' answer once will abandon the app permanently, and no secondary feature or viral receipt card can recover that trust.
rejected_alternatives: Building out a fuller secondary-screen surface area at the cost of core-loop fidelity or the race-condition test
constraints: Later build phases must treat the two core funnels and the accept race-condition test as non-negotiable before investing in secondary screens

decisions.decision: The product promise is locked as: Pulse Relay lets a parent in a school-pickup pod broadcast a same-day pickup coverage need and guarantees exactly one trusted pod member locks it in via server-arbitrated first-accept-wins, with no ambiguity and no silent failure states.
decisions.rationale: Both participants independently converged on near-identical wording across two rounds; it directly reflects the trust-graph/pod mechanic locked in prompt_contract and product_research.
rejected_alternatives: Framing the promise around generic 'matching' or convenience rather than trust-graph coordination
constraints: Naming, onboarding copy, and all future screens must trace back to this exact promise

decisions.decision: Primary user is a parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod, hit by an unplanned same-day pickup conflict, using the app one-handed under real time pressure.
decisions.rationale: Both participants described the same scenario independently; the ~90-second-attention framing directly drives IA requirements (glanceable, minimal reading, one decision per screen).
rejected_alternatives: A broader 'any parent' framing
A leisurely-use, non-urgent framing
constraints: Every core-loop screen must be legible and actionable in a single glance under stress

decisions.decision: The core loop is: post request into pod (no child PII) -> live visibility + push notification deep-link -> accept -> server-arbitrated first-accept-wins -> explicit confirmed/already-covered states -> optional release/reopen -> optional still-open escalation -> complete -> combined audit/receipt record.
decisions.rationale: Both participants converged on this exact sequence including the named states; it operationalizes the race-condition requirement from product_research into an actual UI flow.
rejected_alternatives: A simpler loop without explicit already-covered/reopened/still-open states
constraints: Every named state (confirmed, already-covered, reopened, still-open, error) must be a distinct, visible UI state, not folded into a generic 'pending' or 'done' state

decisions.decision: Accepting a request is a reversible commitment until handoff is marked complete; releasing ("I can no longer cover this") is a first-class action that immediately reopens the request and re-notifies the pod, targeted at under ~30 seconds.
decisions.rationale: An accept state with no way to back out manufactures false confidence for a parent under stress, which is a worse failure mode than the ambiguous group chat this app replaces.
rejected_alternatives: Treating acceptance as final/irreversible with no in-app release mechanism
Treating back-out as a nice-to-have deferred to v2
constraints: This must be built as a core-loop requirement at the same priority as the accept race-condition test, not as secondary polish

decisions.decision: An unfulfilled request must show a visible, time-aware 'still open' state (e.g. elapsed time since posting) with a re-broadcast path, rather than a static pending indicator or silence.
decisions.rationale: A false 'nothing is happening' read on an actually-open request is as dangerous as a false 'confirmed' read, because it hides the time-dependent information a stressed parent needs to decide whether to escalate outside the app.
rejected_alternatives: A generic static 'pending' or 'waiting' label with no elapsed-time signal
Leaving unfulfilled requests with no distinct visible state
constraints: The request card must surface elapsed time, not just a binary open/closed status

decisions.decision: The data model must support multiple simultaneously-open requests per pod, each with independent identity (requester, urgency) and independently acceptable, even though the UI may optimize for a single focused card.
decisions.rationale: Two unrelated families in the same pod can plausibly have a same-day conflict at once; assuming single-active-request at the data layer risks silent queueing, overwriting, or vanishing cards, which directly contradicts the app's core 'no ambiguity' value proposition.
rejected_alternatives: Modeling single-active-request-per-pod as a hard constraint with multi-request support deferred to v2
Leaving concurrent-request behavior undefined and deciding it ad hoc during build
constraints: API contract and data model in the next phase must not assume one open request per pod at any given time

decisions.decision: The pod-creator role is deliberately minimal: create a pod, receive a join code/link, done — no admin console, no member removal UI, no pod settings screen in v1.
decisions.rationale: Matches the build-priority guidance from portfolio_selection that secondary screens get cut before core-loop fidelity; pod administration is real but non-load-bearing work.
rejected_alternatives: Building a full pod-admin console with member management and settings in v1
constraints: Any pod-admin capability (removing a bad actor, editing pod settings) is explicitly deferred to v2, not built now

decisions.decision: No in-app chat/DM thread is permitted; the only communication surface is the request card plus one optional short note, locked at the same non-negotiable tier as the location, child-PII, and payments bans.
decisions.rationale: A messaging feature (read receipts, typing indicators, per-message notifications, history, moderation) is a categorically larger build that would consume the timeline reserved for the two core funnels; if users need to negotiate beyond a short note, the correct action is reposting the request, not adding DMs.
rejected_alternatives: Allowing a lightweight chat/DM thread attached to each request
Treating the no-chat rule as a soft cut-if-time-is-short item rather than a hard boundary
constraints: No later phase may introduce messaging/chat functionality between pod members

decisions.decision: No recurring or scheduled requests in v1 — every relay request is same-day only.
decisions.rationale: Recurring/scheduling introduces calendar logic and state complexity unrelated to the core urgent-relay value proposition.
rejected_alternatives: Supporting recurring or future-dated relay requests in v1
constraints: Data model should not need to represent recurrence or future scheduling for v1

decisions.decision: No payments feature of any kind in v1.
decisions.rationale: The concept is a trust-graph favor exchange among people who already know each other, not a paid marketplace; payments would reintroduce the marketplace/HopSkipDrive trust model explicitly rejected earlier.
rejected_alternatives: Adding an optional tip/payment mechanic to the relay receipt
constraints: No payment processing, balances, or monetary fields in the data model

decisions.decision: There is no persistent, scrollable request-history feed in v1 beyond what the single audit/receipt artifact already provides per completed request.
decisions.rationale: This app is a current-state coordination tool, not a social feed to browse; a history feed adds surface area without serving the core loop.
rejected_alternatives: Building a scrollable history/feed screen of past requests
constraints: Any 'history' surfaced to users should be limited to individual completed-request receipts, not an aggregated feed screen

decisions.decision: Subscription value is locked to exactly three unlocks: multi-pod membership, exportable/signed receipt-and-audit history, and critical-alert-tier notifications that bypass Focus/DND. Response-time analytics and escalation-policy customization are explicitly deferred out of v1.
decisions.rationale: Each of the three locked items maps to a concrete, nameable paying user (the two-school parent, the co-parenting parent needing documentation, the parent who needs pickup pings to break through Focus/DND); the deferred items either don't survive contact with existing safety requirements (capacity tiers are meaningless against a fixed-size pod that already must support multiple free simultaneous requests) or lack a validated concrete user (analytics).
rejected_alternatives: A broader, open-ended 'phased product direction' list including capacity tiers, escalation-policy customization, and response-time analytics
Gating pod capacity or escalation timing behind a paid tier
constraints: No later phase may add subscription unlocks beyond these three without an explicit new decision
Escalation/re-broadcast timing (DEC-initial_discussion-005) and multi-request support (DEC-initial_discussion-006) must remain fully free and unmodified by subscription tier

decisions.decision: The free tier must include every core relay action (post, accept, release, complete, and the resulting audit/receipt artifact) fully and forever for at least one pod; nothing touching the state machine (claimed/already-covered/reopened/still-open/error) may ever be degraded, delayed, or gated behind payment.
decisions.rationale: Gating pickup-coverage safety behavior behind a paywall would be a trust and safety failure, not a normal product growth tradeoff, and would directly contradict this app's entire reason to exist.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving free-vs-paid core-loop boundaries as an implicit assumption to be inferred during architecture/build
constraints: Architecture and build phases must treat this as a hard constraint on the data model and entitlement logic, not a UX nuance

decisions.decision: The viral/growth mechanic is named explicitly as 'the core loop must work flawlessly on every new pod's first real incident' — an unglamorous reliability requirement with no dedicated UI — not the shareable receipt card, which is a secondary proof artifact supporting word-of-mouth but is not itself the growth lever.
decisions.rationale: The receipt card can only fire after a successful completion, so it is a lagging artifact of things already having gone right, not a mechanism that makes things go right; over-investing build time in the card's polish while core-loop reliability has rough edges would misallocate effort against what actually drives pod-level adoption.
rejected_alternatives: Treating the shareable receipt card as the primary viral growth feature
Building a dedicated invite/referral screen as the growth mechanic
constraints: No later phase may introduce an 'invite your pod' or referral screen framed as the primary growth mechanic
First-incident reliability (notification latency, race-condition correctness) must be prioritized in build order ahead of receipt-card visual polish

decisions.decision: No optimistic UI confirmation is permitted anywhere in the client for outcome-affecting actions (accept, release, complete); an explicit 'sending / awaiting confirmation' transitional state must appear between user tap and server acknowledgment, even for a fraction of a second.
decisions.rationale: The product's entire value proposition is that 'confirmed' means the server has actually arbitrated the outcome; a premature optimistic success flash before server ack would recreate the exact false-confidence failure mode the app exists to eliminate from group chats.
rejected_alternatives: Optimistic UI updates for responsiveness, reconciled after the fact with backend state
constraints: This is a hard constraint on the API contract and client state machine in the next (architecture) phase, not a polish item

decisions.decision: The MVP slice for pulse-relay is the entire core loop end-to-end (post, live visibility + push, accept-race arbitration, release/reopen, still-open escalation, complete, audit/receipt) run by two real seeded accounts in one pod — not a stripped-down subset of it.
decisions.rationale: The app has no secondary value proposition to fall back on; a subset that omits race arbitration, release, or still-open escalation is a different, less defensible app that happens to share a name, not a smaller version of pulse-relay.
rejected_alternatives: A smaller slice covering only post-and-accept without race arbitration, release, or still-open escalation
Treating this slice as a screen-by-screen build target rather than one complete incident workflow
constraints: Later build phases must implement this slice as one continuous workflow tested with two real accounts, not as isolated screens

decisions.decision: The accept-race 'already covered by [name]' loser transition is locked as critical-path, non-negotiable-quality UX within this MVP slice, prioritized above other visual work in the slice including the shareable receipt card — it is explicitly carved out of the 'polish-only UI' cut bucket.
decisions.rationale: This is the one moment in the product where 'you didn't get what you tapped for' is the correct, desired outcome, and a generic error-style treatment would read as the app malfunctioning rather than working as designed, directly undermining the trust the whole concept depends on.
rejected_alternatives: Treating the loser-state transition as an equal-priority correctness item alongside all other MVP screens, with visual treatment decided later as generic polish
Bundling this transition into the same cut-list tier as animations, theming, and iconography
constraints: The next design phase must name this transition explicitly and not lump it into generic 'polish' decisions
Build priority within this slice puts this transition's fidelity ahead of receipt-card visual investment

decisions.decision: This MVP slice must use real server-side compare-and-swap arbitration and real APNs-delivered push notifications for the accept-race outcome; polling or client-side arbitration is explicitly disallowed as a stand-in, even if it would satisfy the same UI-state acceptance checklist.
decisions.rationale: A polling-based or client-arbitrated version could pass every listed UI-state test while quietly failing to prove the backend is genuinely load-bearing, which is exactly the failure mode DEC-prompt_contract-004 and DEC-prompt_contract-008 exist to prevent, and would leave the 'push notifications driven by server-side events' backend justification from the original prompt unproven.
rejected_alternatives: Allowing a polling loop or client-side arbitration to stand in for real-time delivery during this slice, deferring real APNs wiring to a later phase
constraints: The build phase's server-side write for accept must be a genuine conditional/compare-and-swap operation, and the winner/loser split must be sourced from that write's result, not inferred client-side
Push delivery in this slice must be real APNs with a working deep link, not simulated or polled

decisions.decision: The acceptance bar for this slice is a literal two-phone side-by-side demo — two real seeded accounts on two real devices where one confirms and the other shows 'already covered by [name]' within a second or two, with zero chat and zero manual reconciliation — with all itemized validation criteria (backend reachability, race-test determinism, push timing, release/reopen timing, still-open aging, force-quit persistence) serving as constituent checks within that demo rather than a separate competing checklist.
decisions.rationale: A spec can pass every itemized criterion in isolation and still fail to produce the 'oh, that's clever' reaction if the pieces don't come together smoothly; naming the physical two-phone demo as the real bar keeps the team focused on the experience the whole concept depends on, not just checkbox completion.
rejected_alternatives: Treating the itemized validation criteria as a flat checklist with no single unifying acceptance demo
constraints: Verification in the build phase should be run and judged as this literal two-device demo, with the itemized criteria checked as part of it

decisions.decision: The client shows honest, literal delivery-count copy on post ('Sent to N pod members') based on actual push registration/token status, with a warning banner if delivery looks uncertain, rather than implying full pod visibility.
decisions.rationale: The free tier has no critical-alert/DND-bypass, so silent notification failure on a new pod's first incident is a real and likely failure mode; pretending otherwise would recreate the false-confidence problem this app exists to eliminate.
rejected_alternatives: Generic 'notification sent' copy that implies everyone was reached
Treating notification reliability as solvable in v1 and deferring the copy decision
constraints: This must be documented as an accepted free-tier limitation, not treated as a bug to be silently patched later

decisions.decision: Same-day cutoffs and elapsed-time/aging calculations are computed entirely server-side using UTC timestamps plus a pod-home-timezone value set once at pod creation; no client-local-time logic is used for these calculations.
decisions.rationale: Per-device local time creates ambiguous same-day boundaries and inconsistent aging displays across devices/timezones, undermining the 'no ambiguity, ever' requirement, especially for co-parenting pods with members in different timezones.
rejected_alternatives: Using device-local time to determine same-day cutoffs or elapsed time
constraints: Pod home timezone must be captured at pod creation and used as the sole reference for date/aging math

decisions.decision: Every outcome-affecting action (post/accept/release/complete/withdraw) carries a client-generated idempotent action ID; the server must handle duplicate submissions idempotently, and any relaunch after a force-quit/crash must reconcile from server truth rather than trusting stale local UI state. A force-quit-mid-accept-before-ack scenario is a named acceptance test alongside the two-phone race demo.
decisions.rationale: Without idempotency, retries or crash-relaunches during outcome-affecting actions could create duplicate requests or leave a device showing an outcome that never actually happened server-side, directly violating the no-false-confirmation principle.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving crash/retry behavior as an implementation detail discovered during build or QA
constraints: This is a hard requirement on the API contract and client state machine in the architecture phase, not a polish item
The force-quit-mid-accept test case must be run and verified, not just described

decisions.decision: The pod-creator role gains exactly one additional capability beyond create-pod-and-get-code: revoke-and-reissue the join code, invalidating the old code immediately on rotation.
decisions.rationale: A permanent, unrevocable join code would make the trust-graph-only matching safety property decorative if a code leaks or is sent to the wrong group; this is a narrow, surgical fix that doesn't reopen the admin-console scope already cut.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving join codes permanent and un-revocable
Building a full pod-admin console with member management to address this
constraints: No other admin/moderation capability is added alongside this one

decisions.decision: A pod with no members other than its creator gets a distinct empty state and CTA ('share the invite') that is visually and semantically separate from 'pod has other members but nobody has responded yet' (re-broadcast/escalate CTA).
decisions.rationale: Collapsing these two very different situations into one generic 'waiting' state would recreate the false-confidence failure mode this app is built to eliminate, since a solo pod and an unresponsive pod require completely different next actions from the user.
rejected_alternatives: A single generic waiting/pending empty state covering both situations
constraints: Design and build phases must treat these as two distinct, named UI states, not variants of the same screen

decisions.decision: The audit/receipt record persists after either party deletes their account, with the departed party rendered as a placeholder (e.g. 'Former member') in both the internal audit view and the shareable projection.
decisions.rationale: The record may serve as custody/co-parenting documentation for the other party; allowing either party to unilaterally erase it via account deletion would undermine the entire evidence model the export feature was built to serve.
rejected_alternatives: Cascading deletion of the audit/receipt record when either party deletes their account
constraints: Account deletion logic must explicitly exclude audit/receipt records from cascading deletes

decisions.decision: UI copy and help text must explicitly state that an 'accepted' request means a trusted pod member has claimed responsibility, never that help or on-time arrival is guaranteed.
decisions.rationale: Without this, users could reasonably infer a stronger guarantee than the app actually provides, especially since v1 has no location/ETA tracking to verify actual arrival.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving this distinction implicit and undocumented
constraints: This must appear as visible copy on the accepted/claimed state, not just be an internal design assumption

decisions.decision: Add a first-class, requester-only terminal `withdrawn` state for same-day requests, usable only while the request is still open/still-open/reopened and unclaimed; it is arbitrated through the same server-side CAS mechanism as accept (so a race between an incoming accept and a withdraw resolves deterministically), triggers a real push/re-notify to the pod, and never generates an audit/receipt artifact. It is visually and semantically distinct from `complete` (e.g. muted/gray 'Withdrawn — no longer needed', not the green completion/receipt state).
decisions.rationale: Without an explicit withdraw path, a self-resolved situation leaves a stale, actively-escalating open request that can lead a good-faith pod member to accept and act on a need that no longer exists — a real-world harm on par with the false-positive-confirmation risk the rest of the state machine is designed to prevent. Auto-closure alone doesn't cover the acute window before expiry kicks in.
rejected_alternatives: Relying solely on bounded auto-closure plus manual re-post, with no requester-facing withdraw action
Treating stale-request cleanup as a passive warning rather than an explicit requester-triggered state
Allowing a generic 'cancel' to behave like or be visually similar to a completed handoff
constraints: `withdrawn` must never generate an audit/receipt artifact, since no handoff occurred
`withdrawn` must use a CAS-arbitrated write and idempotent action IDs like every other outcome-affecting action
`withdrawn` must be visually and copy-wise distinct from `complete` and `error` at the same fidelity bar as the 'already covered' transition

decisions.decision: The `withdrawn` and `release` actions are mutually exclusive by state: withdraw is only ever visible to the requester while the request is open/still-open (unclaimed); once a request is accepted, only the accepter's `release` action is available and withdraw disappears entirely.
decisions.rationale: This eliminates the specific ambiguity risk that motivated hesitation about adding a cancel-like action — a user is never shown an action that could be misread as undoing someone else's commitment, because the two actions never coexist for the same request.
rejected_alternatives: Allowing withdraw to remain visible or available after a request has been accepted
constraints: Client and server logic must enforce this mutual exclusivity as a state-machine invariant, not just a UI convention

decisions.decision: V1 ships with no in-app moderation, reporting, muting, or member-removal capability to handle bad-faith or spam posting by a known pod member; this is an explicit, named, accepted limitation, mitigated only by trust-graph invite-only membership, per-request attribution/auditability, and the creator's code revoke/reissue capability.
decisions.rationale: Building real moderation would reopen the admin-console/member-management scope deliberately cut in earlier phases for good reasons; leaving the risk undocumented would be worse than naming it plainly, consistent with how cold-start and Focus/DND limitations were handled.
rejected_alternatives: Adding member removal, reporting, or rate-limiting capability in v1
Leaving this risk unaddressed and undocumented
constraints: Onboarding/help copy must state plainly that this is a trust-graph, invitation-based tool for known pods, not a moderated public platform
This limitation cannot be used to justify degrading any core-loop guarantee (APNs delivery, receipt integrity, state-machine correctness, four-state screens)

decisions.decision: Must-have features are split into execution-priority tiers for build scheduling only: Tier-1 (auth persistence, zero-state create-or-join onboarding, no-PII posting with awaiting-confirmation, honest delivery-count copy, server-committed push dispatch, and CAS-based accept-race determinism) forms the literal two-phone demo and cannot be rushed; Tier-2 (release/reopen, withdrawn, still-open aging/re-broadcast, completion-to-receipt) remains fully required but may ship with rougher visual polish first if time is short.
decisions.rationale: Both participants agreed the app has no fallback value proposition if the demo-critical race/notification path is wrong, so any time pressure must be absorbed by the less catastrophic parts of the loop, never the part that proves the backend is load-bearing.
rejected_alternatives: Treating all must-have features as equally weighted with no execution order
Making release/withdraw/still-open lower-priority in a way that could drop their correctness, not just their polish
constraints: Tier-2 items remain required outcomes in the graded contract, not optional
Only visual/UX polish may be reduced under time pressure, never state-machine or server-invariant correctness

decisions.decision: Subscription-tier features (multi-pod membership, exportable/signed receipt history, critical-alert notification bypass) are explicitly out of implementation scope for this build: no StoreKit integration, no paywall UI, no core behavior gated behind entitlement.
decisions.rationale: Building paid-tier scaffolding does not increase confidence that the core trust-graph relay works under real concurrent pressure, and would divert time from the one thing this build must prove — real backend-load-bearing, two-device race correctness.
rejected_alternatives: Implementing paywall/subscription screens or entitlement checks in this build
Treating the three unlocks as hidden must-have build tasks
constraints: Any schema entitlement fields must remain inert and unused in this build
No UI may reference or imply an unavailable premium flow

decisions.decision: Tiering is strictly a scheduling/finish-quality mechanism, not a requirements-erosion mechanism: every must-have requirement remains required for acceptance, and all core invariants (CAS arbitration, idempotency, withdraw/release state exclusivity, four-state visibility, server-owned time semantics, no-optimistic terminal confirmation) must be implemented and testable regardless of tier.
decisions.rationale: Prevents a build agent from reading the tiering as license to ship an incomplete or UI-only version of a 'lower tier' state transition under time pressure.
rejected_alternatives: Allowing partial or cosmetic-only implementations of core invariants for Tier-2 items when time is short
constraints: A build that preserves UI layout for a Tier-2 screen but drops or fakes its underlying state transition is non-compliant, regardless of tier

decisions.decision: The tokenized Theme.swift system and full light/dark coverage on every core screen is locked as a hard must-have with design-lint parity — no hardcoded font, size, spacing, or color literal outside the theme file, and no core-screen visual sign-off without both appearances verified.
decisions.rationale: This fleet already has two recorded design-lint incidents matching exactly this failure (hardcoded font size, hardcoded inline color), and the global phase playbook already requires tokenized styling and dark-mode as a hard rule, not a stylistic nicety; leaving it on a 'should' list risked a build agent treating it as optional after spending its budget on core-loop correctness.
rejected_alternatives: Keeping the tokenized theme system on the should/could list
Allowing inline style literals in feature views with cleanup deferred
Treating dark-mode support as a later polish pass
constraints: All core screens must reference Theme.swift for typography/color/spacing
Any screen with non-theme-sourced style literals is out of scope for acceptance

decisions.decision: R-006, R-007, R-009, R-010, R-011, and R-037 are explicitly labeled demo-critical/uncuttable within the requirements contract itself: honest delivery-count copy, the server-side CAS/arbitration path, the deterministic winner/loser split, non-optimistic terminal confirmation, the bounded server-side push-dispatch commitment, and the literal two-device side-by-side demo.
decisions.rationale: Under real schedule pressure a build agent can misjudge which corner is safe to cut; naming the safety-proof requirements explicitly in the document removes that judgment call rather than relying on inferred tiering alone.
rejected_alternatives: Relying on Tier-1/Tier-2 labeling alone to protect the safety-critical subset
Allowing any demo-critical requirement to be downgraded or softened under time pressure
constraints: If any demo-critical requirement is incomplete, the build is non-compliant regardless of progress on Tier-2 items
Architecture and state-machine docs in later phases must carry these six requirements forward as explicitly non-negotiable

decisions.decision: R-007 (push delivery) is locked as a two-part contract: the backend must commit the CAS write and submit the APNs payload within a strict server-owned bound (target <=2s happy-path), while actual device receipt timing is an empirically-observed property of the two-device demo, not a hard API-level pass/fail metric, given Apple's push infrastructure is best-effort.
decisions.rationale: Prevents the requirements document from making an impossible-to-guarantee promise about third-party infrastructure while still holding the backend to strict, verifiable, server-side latency discipline.
rejected_alternatives: Wording the requirement as guaranteed/immediate end-to-end device delivery
Treating any observed APNs delay during the demo as an automatic backend defect
constraints: Backend should target and log server-side dispatch timing as verifiable telemetry
Demo observations of infra-side delay are noted as delivery-UX risk, not treated as a false-positive architecture failure

decisions.decision: The card status palette is locked as amber-pulse for open/awaiting/live requests, warm teal-green (not stoplight green) for confirmed/claimed, slate/muted gray for terminal non-actionable states (withdrawn, complete), with true red reserved exclusively for genuine system/network errors — never used for any normal product state including the accept-race loser.
decisions.rationale: A parent glancing at this screen mid-panic reads color before text; using alarm-register colors (stoplight red/green, sci-fi HUD blue) for normal outcomes would misrepresent the emotional register the whole product promise depends on (relief, not alarm), and would risk the uncuttable already-covered transition reading as a malfunction.
rejected_alternatives: Literal stoplight red/green state coding
Cold blue-black sci-fi/military HUD palette with electric accents
constraints: Theme.swift must define these as semantic color roles, not literals scattered through views
Red may never be used to render 'already covered by [name]' or any other non-error terminal state

decisions.decision: The signature interaction is a pulse-to-latch motion: an open request card pulses on a calm heartbeat rhythm while awaiting server acknowledgment, then converts to a steady locked-panel state on resolution. Both the accept-race winner ('claimed/confirmed') and loser ('already covered by [name]') receive this same fast, mechanical, half-second latch treatment — no shake, no alert icon, no error styling on the loser.
decisions.rationale: The losing side of the accept-race is the one moment in the product where 'you didn't get what you tapped for' is the correct, designed outcome (already flagged demo-critical/uncuttable in app_features); giving it the identical calm-latch treatment as the winner is what makes the two-phone demo read as 'the app worked' rather than 'the app broke' at a glance, without requiring the viewer to read any text.
rejected_alternatives: A plain status-chip text swap with no accompanying motion
Distinct/error-styled treatment for the losing transition (shake, alert icon, red accent)
constraints: Reduce Motion must collapse the pulse/latch to an instant but still visually distinct crossfade, not remove the state distinction entirely
This transition's fidelity takes priority over all other visual polish in the build, per the earlier locked build-priority decisions

decisions.decision: Default SwiftUI chrome is explicitly rejected: no plain List/Form rows, no default NavigationStack system-blue accents, and no transient toast-style confirmation (e.g. a flashing 'Accepted!' that disappears) for any outcome-affecting action.
decisions.rationale: A row-list reads as an inbox and a vanishing toast is exactly the kind of easy-to-miss confirmation this app exists to eliminate; both would recreate the ambiguous-group-chat mental model the product is built to replace.
rejected_alternatives: Standard List/Form-based request feed with system accent color
Toast/alert-based confirmation for accept/release/complete/withdraw
constraints: All outcome-affecting states must be persistent, baked into the card itself, sourced only from real backend acknowledgment

decisions.decision: Screen scope stays deliberately narrow: session/auth gate, pod onboarding (create or join with true empty states), the live relay board, request composer, request detail (accept/release/withdraw), receipt, and minimal profile/pod-settings — no additional branching or surface area.
decisions.rationale: Matches the build-priority guidance locked in portfolio_selection and app_features: this phase's entire purpose is eliminating claim/no-claim ambiguity, and any added screens or navigation branches would compete with that fidelity for build time.
rejected_alternatives: Adding richer navigation, tabs, or additional secondary screens at this stage
constraints: Any future screen proposal must justify itself against directly reducing false-certainty or missed-coverage risk in the core loop

decisions.decision: The design language's final name is 'Relay HUD.' The pulse-to-latch motion is the signature interaction within it, not a second brand name, and should be reflected in code as a concrete component name (e.g. BeaconCard/RelayBeaconView).
decisions.rationale: A shorter, single name is what actually gets used in docs, code, and UI copy dozens of times through the build; 'Beacon' surviving as the literal name of the reusable motion component gives build agents a greppable identifier instead of a second competing brand term.
rejected_alternatives: 'Relay Beacon HUD' as the full product design-language name
Two parallel names (HUD for structure, Beacon for motion) with no clear precedence
constraints: Design docs, Theme file comments, and onboarding copy should refer to the language as Relay HUD
The pulse-to-latch component should carry 'Beacon' in its SwiftUI type name

decisions.decision: Secondary screens (receipt, profile/sign-out, pod settings/code rotation) inherit Theme tokens, spacing, typography, and state language but are explicitly barred from: custom entrance/exit transitions beyond the system default, bespoke empty-state illustration work (a plain SF Symbol plus one line of Theme-styled text is the ceiling), and any color treatment outside the shared semantic palette. The receipt card is a narrow exception only in that it gets a higher bar for typography and information hierarchy (since it leaves the app via the share sheet), but still receives no second signature animation.
decisions.rationale: Turning 'utility-only' into named, specific bans prevents a build agent with spare time from investing craft budget into a secondary screen's own micro-interaction, which would come directly at the expense of the accept-race card's fidelity — the one thing this app is actually judged on.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving secondary-screen restraint as a soft 'keep it small' instruction with no named boundaries
Allowing the receipt card its own signature motion given its external-facing role
constraints: Any secondary-screen work proposing custom motion or bespoke illustration is out of scope for this build
The receipt card's added craft budget is limited to typography/layout quality, not animation

decisions.decision: The live board's default 'all clear' resting state — no open requests, quiet pod — is a real, composed screen: pod name, member count, an at-rest (non-pulsing) 'all clear' indicator using the same slate/teal semantic language, and the post-request CTA as the single obvious action. It does not get its own unique signature motion, but it must not be a blank view or a bare icon-plus-button placeholder.
decisions.rationale: This is the single most-viewed screen in the app given pulse-relay's rare-but-critical usage pattern (named in round one as a core risk); an unfinished-looking resting state would make the whole app read as unfinished even if the high-stress states are polished, and directly violates the already-locked global rule that empty states are designed content, not blank views.
rejected_alternatives: Treating the resting state as a trivial placeholder screen since all design energy goes to the high-stress states
Giving the resting state its own signature motion, which would violate the secondary/non-critical-screen austerity principle
constraints: The resting state must use the same Theme tokens and semantic palette as the active board, at rest rather than pulsing
This screen is exempt from the 'zero unique motion' secondary-screen rule only in that it needs real composed content, not in that it needs its own animation

decisions.decision: If build time is constrained, visual/motion craft budget is spent in this strict order: (1) the open-to-awaiting pulse, (2) the deterministic winner/loser latch resolution, (3) completed/withdrawn terminal card clarity — with everything else (secondary screens, resting state) built plain and correct rather than polished.
decisions.rationale: Names an explicit tiebreak so a build agent under deadline pressure doesn't have to guess where to cut visual finish, directly extending the Tier-1/Tier-2 execution-priority logic already locked in app_features into concrete design-craft terms.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving craft-budget prioritization implicit and inferred from the rest of this phase's output
constraints: No craft time should go to secondary-screen polish before all three named priorities are fully realized

decisions.decision: Codex's structured DESIGN SPEC (type scale, spacing grid, component inventory, navigation map, motion/haptics, accessibility) is adopted as the canonical base for this phase, extended with Claude's client-state-machine layer rather than replaced by a competing token set.
decisions.rationale: Codex's pass was the more fully-worked-out formal document hitting every required playbook heading; Claude explicitly conceded this rather than defending her own alternate numbers, so rewriting from scratch would only create churn and regression risk in a constrained build.
rejected_alternatives: Maintaining two parallel token sets and reconciling per-value
Rewriting the spec around Claude's alternate type/spacing/color values
constraints: Any further palette changes must be surgical edits to Codex's existing token file, not a wholesale replacement

decisions.decision: The request/card state machine distinguishes awaitingConfirmation (this device's own action in flight) from reconciling (state learned via a push-triggered refetch) as separate internal states sharing the pulse visual, plus queuedOffline (action taken with no connection, not yet in flight) and a distinct 'no longer open' state for a deep-link that resolves to a withdrawn/expired request — all four folded into the formal per-screen spec, not left as an inferred edge case.
decisions.rationale: Collapsing awaitingConfirmation and reconciling into one case would make the losing device in the accept-race snap straight to 'already covered' with no pulse, destroying the exact side-by-side visual proof the two-phone demo depends on; queuedOffline and the expired-deep-link state prevent false or scary-looking states for two situations (offline compose, stale notification taps) that will happen routinely in real use.
rejected_alternatives: Treating reconciling as the same internal case as awaitingConfirmation
Rendering a queued offline action as a generic awaiting-confirmation spinner
Rendering an expired/withdrawn deep-link target as a generic error state
constraints: Build must implement all four as named, distinct internal states, not just visually similar variants of two states

decisions.decision: Screen graph and navigation are locked: AppGate resolves to AuthGate, PodOnboarding, or RelayBoard (default root); RelayBoard presents RequestComposer and RequestDetail as sheets, with RequestDetail also serving as the push deep-link destination; Profile and PodSettings are reachable only via stack push from the board header. No tabs, no additional navigation branches.
decisions.rationale: Matches the narrow-screen-scope discipline already locked in design_discussion and keeps the IA aligned with the app's actual single-core-loop workload rather than adding chrome for an app with essentially one screen that matters.
rejected_alternatives: A tab-based root
Additional top-level navigation branches beyond the core loop and two secondary screens
constraints: No later phase may add tabs or additional root-level navigation destinations

decisions.decision: Motion timing is locked: the open-to-awaiting pulse is a 0.9s ease-in-out repeating breathing animation (scale 0.99→1.02 plus border alpha oscillation); resolution to either winner or loser uses an identical 0.45s mechanical spring latch (response 0.45, damping 0.82); Reduce Motion collapses both to a ~0.15s crossfade that preserves the text/icon state change; haptics never differentiate winner from loser as success versus warning/error.
decisions.rationale: Codifies design_discussion's requirement that the accept-race loser reads as 'worked as designed' rather than a malfunction, down to exact animation and haptic values a build agent can implement without inventing anything.
rejected_alternatives: Distinct or error-styled haptic/motion treatment for the losing transition
constraints: No implementation may give the loser transition a different duration, curve, or haptic category than the winner

decisions.decision: If build time is constrained, visual/motion craft effort is spent in this order: (1) the open-to-awaiting pulse, (2) the winner/loser latch resolution, (3) completed/withdrawn terminal card clarity — before any polish on the board resting state or secondary screens.
decisions.rationale: Directly carries forward the craft-budget tiebreak already locked in design_discussion into this phase's concrete spec, so a build agent under deadline pressure has an explicit order rather than having to infer one.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving craft-budget priority unstated in this phase's own spec and relying solely on the prior phase's mention of it
constraints: No craft time goes to secondary-screen or resting-state polish before all three named priorities are fully realized

decisions.decision: Push notification payloads are never rendered directly as UI state; arrival only triggers an authoritative refetch of that specific request, and the card transitions only after that fetch resolves. This must appear as its own explicit written architectural rule in the spec, not merely be implied by the existence of the 'reconciling' state.
decisions.rationale: The fast, obvious implementation path for a competent iOS engineer is to decode and render the notification payload directly, which is less code than triggering a fetch; that shortcut would pass every screenshot review and even a casual demo while silently failing the CAS race-condition guarantee the first time APNs delivers pushes out of order or drops one.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving this as an implied consequence of the reconciling state's name without a standalone written rule
constraints: The final design-spec document must state this rule explicitly alongside the other interaction invariants (no optimistic UI, etc.), not leave it inferable only from the state list

decisions.decision: The Relay HUD surface/neutral system is corrected to a warm-neutral palette (warm off-white backgrounds, warm charcoal dark surfaces) replacing the cool-blue scaffold from the earlier draft, while all state accent colors (amber pulse, teal confirmed, slate terminal, error red) remain unchanged.
decisions.rationale: The neutral scaffolding, not the state accents, was the remaining source of the 'cold blue-black sci-fi HUD' register explicitly rejected in design_discussion's DEC-design_discussion-001; a cold base can trigger an alarm register even when state accents are correct.
rejected_alternatives: Keeping the blue-leaning neutral tokens on the grounds that state accents were already correct
Claude's independently-proposed alternate warm hex values, treated as confirming the same fix rather than a competing spec since both point the same direction
constraints: All base surface/divider/background/card tones in Theme.swift must use the warm-neutral values in the final palette table
No non-tokenized neutral literals anywhere outside Theme.swift

decisions.decision: Relay board request ordering is exclusively server-authoritative displayOrder (created-at ascending plus a deterministic backend tie-break); no client-side urgency computation or local re-sort exists anywhere in the spec.
decisions.rationale: No urgency/severity/priority field exists anywhere in the locked data model; leaving 'urgency' in the spec language would hand a build agent an undefined sort key it would have to invent or silently drop, violating the playbook rule that no adjective may stand in for a number.
rejected_alternatives: Retaining 'sorted by urgency then age' as descriptive shorthand for age-driven sorting
Allowing client-side re-sorting as a fallback
constraints: Board component renders request IDs in exact backend response order
Any future urgency concept requires an explicit new data-model decision in a later phase, not implicit inclusion here

decisions.decision: Push notification payloads are never rendered as authoritative request state; every push is treated strictly as a wake-up signal that must trigger a targeted authoritative refetch of that specific request before any card transition occurs, and this is written as its own explicit architectural rule in the spec.
decisions.rationale: Decoding and rendering directly from the notification payload is the fastest, most obvious implementation path for a competent iOS engineer, and it would pass every screenshot review and casual demo while silently breaking CAS correctness the first time APNs delivers pushes out of order or drops one — exactly the failure this app's core value proposition depends on not happening.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving the rule implicit in the existence of the 'reconciling' state without a standalone written line
constraints: RequestDetail transitions to any terminal state must be gated on a real fetch result, never on notification userInfo contents
'reconciling' remains an explicit, named state between wake-up and applied fetch result

decisions.decision: Connectivity and freshness edge cases are locked as explicit, named spec elements: queuedOffline is a state distinct from awaitingConfirmation; a single top-level (not per-card) 'Syncing latest pod state…' banner appears on launch/foreground and after a force-quit mid-action until the first fresh fetch of the session lands, with stale cache still rendering underneath for continuity; the elapsed-timer chip reads MM:SS under one hour then 'Xh Ym'; and the connection/session banner carries two distinct copy states (offline-with-queued-actions vs. uncertain-delivery) rather than one generic message.
decisions.rationale: These are real, routinely-occurring situations (cold launch after force-quit mid-accept, spotty connectivity, sub-hour same-day timers) that directly affect user trust in what the screen is telling them, and leaving them implicit invites a build agent to render stale state with false confidence or collapse two meaningfully different situations into one vague message.
rejected_alternatives: Treating queuedOffline as a visual variant of awaitingConfirmation
A per-card syncing indicator instead of one top-level banner
An HH:MM:SS elapsed-timer format
A single generic 'connection issue' banner covering both offline-queued and uncertain-delivery cases
constraints: Board-level syncing banner must appear whenever data freshness for the session is unverified
No terminal (latched/completed/withdrawn) card may be presented with full visual confidence before the first post-launch sync completes
No HH:MM:SS timer format anywhere in the app

decisions.decision: No external Claude Design pass is used for this build; the design_handoff spec is implemented directly in SwiftUI, with the previously drafted upload prompt retained only as a future fallback for static, post-implementation assets (e.g. App Store imagery), never as part of the build's design-to-code path.
decisions.rationale: The product's actual value lives in an interaction state machine (pulse/latch parity between the accept-race winner and loser), which a static mockup tool cannot represent or validate; a polished set of frames risks being mistaken for a validated interaction when it proves nothing about the one behavior this app is judged on.
rejected_alternatives: Commissioning an external Claude Design pass before build as an optional handoff-visual step
constraints: Any future static-asset generation from the retained prompt must happen only after interaction implementation is complete and must not omit the reconciling/queuedOffline/deep-link-expired states

decisions.decision: The canonical warm-neutral hex values are Codex's round-3 token set (background #F8F3EE/#121821, surface.card #FFFDF9/#1A2430, surface.strong #F2E9DD/#24303F, surface.divider #E7D9CA/#2E3F50, text.primary #2A221A/#EFF4FA, text.secondary #5B4E43/#9FA8B2, text.muted #7C7168/#87909A), adopted over Claude's independently-proposed alternate warm values since both target the identical fix and Codex's set was already the complete, fully-integrated token file.
decisions.rationale: Two near-identical warm-neutral proposals arrived in the same round from parallel drafting; picking one concrete, already-fully-specified set avoids a further round over a few hex digits when both authors agree on the substantive direction.
rejected_alternatives: Running a fourth round solely to reconcile two very similar warm-neutral hex proposals
constraints: Theme.swift must use exactly these hex pairs for the five neutral roles listed

decisions.decision: Adopt an actor-based RequestSyncCoordinator as the sole mutator of request state and push/queue reconciliation, with all in-flight transitions driven through a single deterministic reducer and an immutable enum state model (not booleans).
decisions.rationale: Push wake-up and local user actions are concurrent by design; an actor plus enum-driven reducer makes illegal/racy state combinations structurally impossible rather than merely conventionally avoided, which is essential for the two-device accept-race proof to hold under real timing.
rejected_alternatives: Plain class/ObservableObject coordinator with shared-state mutation across multiple async paths
Boolean flag combinations for card states
constraints: All request-card phase transitions must flow through the reducer/actor; no ad-hoc state flags anywhere in the client

decisions.decision: Session/auth material used by background refetch and force-quit-reconcile flows is stored in Keychain with accessibility kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly.
decisions.rationale: Push wake-ups routinely arrive while the phone is locked; default whenUnlocked accessibility would silently block the authoritative refetch exactly when reconciliation matters most, directly undermining the 'flawless first incident' bar.
rejected_alternatives: Default whenUnlocked Keychain accessibility
Storing session tokens outside Keychain
constraints: Background wake-triggered fetch path must be designed and tested against a locked-device scenario

decisions.decision: Remote notification authorization is requested only after successful sign-in and pod onboarding, with an explicit one-line rationale shown first; notification action buttons that trigger network actions directly are prohibited — deep-link-to-app is the only interaction surface from a push.
decisions.rationale: Requesting permission before the user has context risks an unrecoverable denial; action buttons in Notification Center would let a build agent bypass the no-optimistic-confirmation contract since the notification center cannot render an awaiting-confirmation state.
rejected_alternatives: Requesting notification permission at cold launch
Notification action buttons (e.g. inline Accept) for accept/release/withdraw
constraints: Every outcome shown to the user must come from a refetched, authoritative server state — never from notification payload or notification-center action results

decisions.decision: Critical Alerts entitlement remains fully unimplemented in v1 and is explicitly documented as feasibility-uncertain for a childcare-pickup-coordination app, not assumed to be obtainable in future roadmap language.
decisions.rationale: Apple grants this entitlement selectively, historically to health/safety/security use cases with demonstrated need; treating it as a guaranteed future unlock would be a false dependency for the already-deferred DND-bypass subscription feature.
rejected_alternatives: Assuming the entitlement is obtainable and wiring related logic now
Adding entitlement-dependent branches into core v1 logic
constraints: No v1 runtime code path may depend on Critical Alerts; any future pursuit must start with an Apple approval feasibility check

decisions.decision: SwiftData board/request/receipt snapshots are treated as a disposable cache (purge-and-refetch on schema mismatch, no hand-rolled migration plan), while queued offline outbox actions must be durable enough to survive relaunch and app-version upgrades without silent loss — preserved separately or routed to an explicit recovery flow if a hard cache reset is required.
decisions.rationale: Server is the sole source of truth for arbitration, so cache volatility is acceptable and cheap, but silently losing a user's queued intent (an accept/release/withdraw they already committed to) is a correctness failure, not an acceptable simplification.
rejected_alternatives: Building a full custom SwiftData migration plan for a cache that doesn't need persistence guarantees
Dropping queued outbox actions silently on cache invalidation
constraints: On startup, stale cache renders for continuity only; terminal-state confidence requires a completed fresh fetch
Outbox durability must be verified across simulated app-version upgrade/relaunch scenarios

decisions.decision: A backend-only concurrent integration test suite is required as an independent acceptance gate: two simultaneous HTTP accept calls against a real (test) CAS endpoint instance must deterministically yield exactly one success and one conflict response, plus a companion accept-vs-withdraw race test, both run with enough concurrency pressure to rule out a pass-by-luck result.
decisions.rationale: A UI-driven two-simulator race test is subject to incidental timing jitter and can pass or fail by luck; only a dedicated backend-level concurrency test actually proves the database transaction/CAS logic is sound, independent of client wiring.
rejected_alternatives: Relying solely on the manual two-device demo as proof of CAS correctness
Treating a passing UI race test as sufficient mechanism verification
constraints: This test must exist and pass before architecture/build signoff, in addition to (not instead of) the manual two-phone demo

decisions.decision: No ML/AR/LLM stack and no third-party dependency expansion beyond Apple system frameworks (URLSession, SwiftData, AuthenticationServices, UserNotifications, OSLog) unless a specific, documented exception materially reduces CAS/push-path risk.
decisions.rationale: The product's hard problem is state arbitration and reliability, not intelligent features; adding model-heavy or third-party tooling increases risk surface without addressing the actual failure modes this app must prove it avoids.
rejected_alternatives: Third-party networking/ORM libraries for developer convenience
Adding LLM/vision/AR hooks in v1
constraints: Any future dependency proposal must include a one-line justification tied to CAS/push-path risk reduction, per the approved tech stack policy

decisions.decision: The primary push-driven reconciliation trigger is a visible alert push plus tap-driven deep link, or a foreground/background scenePhase-triggered refetch; silent content-available push is treated strictly as a best-effort bonus, never the backbone the app depends on for correctness.
decisions.rationale: iOS can throttle or outright suppress silent background push under Low Power Mode or aggressive battery/thermal conditions, which is outside the app's control; leaning on it as the primary reconciliation path would make the 'flawless first incident' requirement depend on infrastructure behavior nobody can guarantee.
rejected_alternatives: Treating background content-available push as the primary reconciliation mechanism with visible push as a fallback
constraints: Foreground/background scenePhase transitions must always trigger a board refetch regardless of whether a silent push was received

decisions.decision: Canonical domain naming is the plain 'Request'-based family (Request, RequestStatus, RequestAction, ActionType, ActionResult, Receipt, Pod, PodMembership, User) rather than a Relay-prefixed family.
decisions.rationale: Both participants independently landed here after swapping preferences mid-round-2; on reflection the plain family doesn't collide with anything in Foundation, avoids Hungarian-notation-style prefix repetition across every domain noun, and keeps types concise for both client and backend workers.
rejected_alternatives: Relay-prefixed family (RelayRequest, RelayAction, RelayReceipt, etc.)
Keeping two parallel naming sets and reconciling per-type
constraints: All build lanes must use exactly this naming; no lane may reintroduce a Relay-prefixed domain type

decisions.decision: Expired-vs-withdrawn is represented by keeping RequestStatus at exactly 5 values (open, claimed, reopened, withdrawn, completed) and adding a separate closeReason: RequestCloseReason? field (autoExpired, requesterWithdrawn, systemHousekeeping), rather than adding a 6th status value.
decisions.rationale: Cleanly separates 'what state is this row in' from 'why did it get here,' keeps the state-machine small, and leaves room for future system-driven reasons without ever touching the status enum again; the client's existing withdrawn card phase reads closeReason to pick copy so no 12th RequestCardPhase case is needed.
rejected_alternatives: Expanding RequestStatus to 6 values including a standalone 'expired' case
Silently dropping the expired/withdrawn distinction entirely
constraints: RequestCardPhase must stay at exactly the 11 states locked in design_handoff
Auto-closure of a stale same-day request sets status=withdrawn plus closeReason=autoExpired, never a new status value

decisions.decision: ActionType includes a required 6th case, reBroadcast, requester-only, allowed only from open/reopened status.
decisions.rationale: DEC-initial_discussion-005 explicitly requires a re-broadcast path for an unfulfilled request; this had been dropped in one round-1 draft and needed to be explicitly restored and locked in both drafts.
rejected_alternatives: Treating re-broadcast as passive aging text with no user-triggered action
Overloading release or withdraw semantics to cover re-broadcast
constraints: reBroadcast uses the same CAS-guarded action-write path as every other action type and updates lastRebroadcastAt

decisions.decision: expectedRequestRevision is a required, non-optional UInt64 parameter on the action-write path (performAction and POST /requests/{id}/actions), threaded from OutboxAction through the coordinator to the wire endpoint; it stays optional only inside OutboxAction's storage model because that same model also queues brand-new post actions with no prior revision to guard.
decisions.rationale: Prevents an offline device's queued action from replaying against an already-terminalized row with ambiguous results; making the parameter optional at the coordinator/API layer would let a future call site silently pass nil and defeat the entire guard.
rejected_alternatives: Optional expectedRequestRevision at the coordinator/API layer
Relying solely on the SQL WHERE clause without a corresponding required API parameter
constraints: Every non-post action call must supply expectedRequestRevision; the coordinator must reject any call site that omits it for accept/release/withdraw/complete/reBroadcast

decisions.decision: A third mandatory verification tier is added: a local coordinator-concurrency test where two independent RequestSyncCoordinator actor instances, each with a distinct fake identity, race an accept call via TaskGroup against one shared local test-backend instance, asserting the winner's event stream emits latchedConfirmed and the loser's emits latchedAlreadyCovered with the correct name populated.
decisions.rationale: Neither the backend-only HTTP concurrency test nor the manual two-phone demo exercises the actual reducer and coordinator under real concurrent server responses; this tier is cheap to run in CI on every commit and is the only test that proves the reducer, coordinator, and real backend agree on the winner together, not each verified in isolation.
rejected_alternatives: Relying only on the backend HTTP concurrency test plus the manual two-phone demo
constraints: This test tier must exist and pass before build signoff, in addition to (not instead of) the other two verification tiers already locked in ios_architecture_review

decisions.decision: GET /api/v1/health is a required endpoint and must be the first call the client makes, gating any backend-dependent routing or state trust on canOperate/apiRevision/minClientVersion.
decisions.rationale: Operationalizes the standing requirement (DEC-prompt_contract-008) that backend reachability be proven before any concept-specific schema or screen is trusted, as a concrete, testable contract-version handshake rather than an assumption.
rejected_alternatives: Assuming backend reachability without an explicit health/version-gate call
Deferring the reachability proof to ad hoc manual testing
constraints: No backend-dependent screen or state may be trusted before this call succeeds

decisions.decision: POST /api/v1/pods/join enforces a hard server-side single-pod-per-account cap in v1, returning 403 already_in_pod for a user with any existing PodMembership.
decisions.rationale: Entitlement-gated multi-pod membership is explicitly out of implementation scope for this build (DEC-app_features-002); the only honest behavior is a hard server-side rejection rather than a silent allow that quietly builds an unrequested multi-pod feature.
rejected_alternatives: Silently allowing a second pod join with no server-side check
Leaving multi-pod-join behavior undefined and deciding it ad hoc during build
constraints: This cap must be enforced server-side, not just hidden client-side

decisions.decision: Board ordering uses a single BIGSERIAL-backed displayOrder column as the sole sort key, exposed under that exact wire field name, with no compound tie-break and no client-side re-sort.
decisions.rationale: A serial column can never produce a tie, so there's no tie-break logic to write, test, or get subtly wrong later; the wire field name matches what design_handoff already locked (DEC-design_handoff-008).
rejected_alternatives: A compound tie-break of createdAtUtc plus (serverRevision, id)
A separate client-visible 'sequence' field distinct from the locked 'displayOrder' name
constraints: Board component must render request IDs in exact backend response order; any future urgency concept requires a new explicit decision

decisions.decision: RequestAction is a standalone, first-class audit-log table, written for every action attempt (post/accept/release/withdraw/complete/reBroadcast) regardless of applied-or-conflict outcome, and is never owned by or nested inside the Receipt object.
decisions.rationale: Withdrawn and expired requests never produce a receipt by explicit prior design, so if the only place an action trail lived was nested inside a conditionally-absent receipt, every accept attempt on a request that ends in withdraw/expiry — including a losing accept that got a genuine conflict — would have no queryable record anywhere, violating the prompt_contract requirement that the audit/event log be a first-class object.
rejected_alternatives: Nesting an action trail array only inside the Receipt struct
